# [Sunday 16 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/16/)

(Lord’s day). Lay long talking with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in bed, then up with great content and to my chamber to set right a picture or two, [Lovett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8522/) having sent me yesterday Sancta Clara’s head [varnished](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13821/), which is very fine, and now my closet is so full stored, and so fine, as I would never desire to have it better.

Dined without any strangers with me, which I do not like on Sundays. Then after dinner by water to Westminster to see [Mrs. Martin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/), whom I found up in her chamber and ready to go abroad. I sat there with her and her husband and others a pretty while, and then away to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there walked up and down to [the Queen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) side, and there saw my dear [Lady Castlemayne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/), who continues admirable, methinks, and I do not hear but that [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) is the same to her still as ever. Anon to chapel, by the King’s closet, and heard a very good anthemne. Then with [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) to [Sir W. Coventry’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) chamber; and there we sat with him and talked. He is weary of anything to do, he says, in the Navy. He tells us this Committee of Accounts will enquire sharply into our office. And, speaking of [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), he says he will not bear any body’s faults but his own. He discoursed as bad of [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) almost, and cries out upon the discipline of the fleete, which is lost, and that there is not in any of the fourth rates and under scarce left one Sea Commander, but all young gentlemen; and what troubles him, he hears that the gentlemen give out that in two or three years a Tarpaulin shall not dare to look after being better than a Boatswain. Which he is troubled at, and with good reason, and at this day [Sir Robert Holmes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/930/) is mighty troubled that [his brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10043/) do not command in chief, but is commanded by [Captain Hannum](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10194/), who, Sir W. Coventry says, he believes to be at least of as good blood, is a longer bred seaman, an elder officer, and an elder commander, but such is Sir R. Holmes’s pride as never to be stopt, he being greatly troubled at my Lord Bruncker’s late discharging all his men and officers but the standing officers at [Chatham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/643/), and so are all other Commanders, and a very great cry hath been to the King from them all in [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) absence. But Sir W. Coventry do undertake to defend it, and my Lord Bruncker got ground I believe by it, who is angry at Sir W. Batten’s and [Sir W. Pen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) bad words concerning it, and I have made it worse by telling him that they refuse to sign to a paper which he and I signed on Saturday to declare the reason of his actions, which Sir W. Coventry likes and would have it sent him and he will sign it, which pleases me well.

So we parted, and I with Lord Bruncker to [Sir P. Neale’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2309/) chamber, and there sat and talked awhile, [Sir Edward Walker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/856/) being there, and telling us how he hath lost many fine rowles of antiquity in heraldry by the late fire, but hath saved the most of his papers. Here was also [Dr. Wallis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10643/), the famous scholar and mathematician; but he promises little.

Left them, and in the dark and cold home by water, and so to supper and to read and so to bed, my eyes being better to-day, and I cannot impute it to anything but by my being much in the dark to-night, for I plainly find that it is only excess of light that makes my eyes sore.

This afternoon I walked with Lord Bruncker into [the Park](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/) and there talked of the times, and he do think that the King sees that he cannot never have much more money or good from this [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/), and that therefore he may hereafter dissolve them, that as soon as he has the money settled he believes a peace will be clapped up, and that there are overtures of a peace, which if such as the [Lord Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/) can excuse he will take. For it is the Chancellor’s interest, he says, to bring peace again, for in peace he can do all and command all, but in war he cannot, because he understands not the nature of the war as to the management thereof. He tells me he do not believe the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) will go to sea again, though there are a great many about the King that would be glad of any occasion to take him out of the world, he standing in their ways; and seemed to mean the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/), who spends his time the most viciously and idly of any man, nor will be fit for any thing; yet bespeaks as if it were not impossible but the King would own him for his son, and that there was a marriage between his mother and him; which God forbid should be if it be not true, nor will the Duke of York easily be gulled in it. But this put to our other distractions makes things appear very sad, and likely to be the occasion of much confusion in a little time, and my Lord Bruncker seems to say that nothing can help us but the King’s making a peace soon as he hath this money; and thereby putting himself out of debt, and so becoming a good husband, and then he will neither need this nor any other Parliament, till he can have one to his mind: for no Parliament can, as he says, be kept long good, but they will spoil one another, and that therefore it hath been the practice of kings to tell Parliaments what he hath for them to do, and give them so long time to do it in, and no longer.

[Harry Kembe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5702/), one of our messengers, is lately dead.

# [Monday 17 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/17/)

Up, and several people to speak with me, and then comes [Mr. Caesar](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8104/), and then [Goodgroome](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2745/), and, what with one and the other, nothing but musique with me this morning, to my great content; and the more, to see that God Almighty hath put me into condition to bear the charge of all this. So out to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and did a little business, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), where they two musicians and [Mr. Cooke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1192/) come to see me, and [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) to go along with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) this afternoon to a play. To dinner, and then our company all broke up, and to my chamber to do several things. Among other things, to write a letter to my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), it being one of the burdens upon my mind that I have not writ to him since he went into Spain, but now I do intend to give him a brief account of our whole year’s actions since he went, which will make amends. My wife well home in the evening from the play; which I was glad of, it being cold and dark, and she having her necklace of [pearl](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14123/) on, and none but Mercer with her. Spent the evening in fitting my books, to have the number set upon each, in order to my having an alphabet of my whole, which will be of great ease to me. This day [Captain Batters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7787/) come from sea in his [fireship](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10129/) and come to see me, poor man, as his patron, and a poor painful wretch he is as can be. After supper to bed.

# [Tuesday 18 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/18/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where I hear the ill news that poor [Batters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7787/), that had been born and bred a seaman, and brought up his ship from sea but yesterday, was, going down from me to his ship, drowned in the [Thames](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/), which is a sad fortune, and do make me afeard, and will do, more than ever I was.

At noon dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and then by coach to my [Lord Bellasses](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8186/), but not at home. So to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), where the Lords are sitting still, I to see [Mrs. Martin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/), who is very well, and intends to go abroad to-morrow after her childbed. She do tell me that this child did come is ‘meme jour that it ought to hazer after my avoir ete con elle before her marid did venir home … [And she would now have done anything cum ego; and did endeavour, but su cosa stava mala, which did empescar. – L&M] Thence to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), and there I sent for [Sarah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8177/), and mighty merry we were … [but contra my will were very far from hazer algo. – L&M] So to [Sir Robert Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) about my [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/), and carried home another dozen of plates, which makes my stock of plates up 2 1/2 dozen, and at home find [Mr. Thomas Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/), with whom I staid and talked a little and invited him to dine with me at [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), and then I to the office, and there late doing business, and so home and to bed. Sorry for poor Batters.

# [Wednesday 19 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/19/)

Up, and by water down to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there with the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) did our usual business, but nothing but complaints of want of money [without] success, and [Sir W. Coventry’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) complaint of the defects of our office (indeed [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/)) without any amendment, and he tells us so plainly of the Committee of [Parliament’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) resolution to enquire home into all our managements that it makes me resolve to be wary, and to do all things betimes to be ready for them. Thence going away met [Mr. Hingston](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10654/) the organist (my old acquaintance) in the Court, and I took him to the [Dog Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/400/) and got him to set me a bass to my [“It is decreed,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10288/) which I think will go well, but he commends the song not knowing the words, but says the ayre is good, and believes the words are plainly expressed. He is of my mind against having of 8ths unnecessarily in composition. This did all please me mightily. Then to talk of [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) family. He says many of the musique are ready to starve, they being five years behindhand for their wages; nay, [Evens](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10655/), the famous man upon the [Harp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/714/) having not his equal in the world, did the other day die for mere want, and was fain to be buried at the almes of the parish, and carried to his grave in the dark at night without one [linke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/), but that Mr. Hingston met it by chance, and did give 12 _d._ to buy two or three links. He says all must come to ruin at this rate, and I believe him.

Thence I up to the [Lords’ House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/) to enquire for [Lord Bellasses](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8186/); and there hear how at a conference this morning between the two Houses about the business of the [Canary Company](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10425/), my [Lord Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2558/) leaning rudely over my [Lord Marquis Dorchester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10532/), my Lord Dorchester removed his elbow. Duke of Buckingham asked him whether he was uneasy; Dorchester replied, yes, and that he durst not do this were he any where else: Buckingham replied, yes he would, and that he was a better man than himself; Dorchester answered that he lyed. With this Buckingham struck off his hat, and took him by his [periwigg](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/517/), and pulled it aside, and held him. My [Lord Chamberlain](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/671/) and others interposed, and, upon coming into the House, the Lords did order them both to [the Tower](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/167/), whither they are to go this afternoon.

I down into [the Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and there the [Lieutenant of the Tower](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1156/) took me with him, and would have me to the Tower to dinner; where I dined at the head of his table, next [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9396/), who is comely and seeming sober and stately, but very proud and very cunning, or I am mistaken, and wanton, too. This day’s work will bring the Lieutenant of the Tower 350 _l._. But a strange, conceited, vain man he is that ever I met withal, in his own praise, as I have heretofore observed of him. Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and upon [Tower Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1395/) saw about 3 or 400 seamen get together; and one, standing upon a pile of bricks, made his sign, with his handkercher, upon his stick, and called all the rest to him, and several shouts they gave. This made me afeard; so I got home as fast as I could. And hearing of no present hurt did go to [Sir Robert Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) about my [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/) again, and coming home do hear of 1000 seamen said in the streets to be in armes. So in great fear home, expecting to find a tumult about my house, and was doubtful of my riches there. But I thank God I found all well. But by and by [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) and [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/) do tell me, that the seamen have been at some prisons, to release some seamen, and the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) is in armes, and all the Guards at the other end of the town; and the Duke of Albemarle is gone with some forces to [Wapping](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2469/), to quell the seamen; which is a thing of infinite disgrace to us.

I sat long talking with them; and, among other things, Sir R. Ford did make me understand how the [House of Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/) is a beast not to be understood, it being impossible to know beforehand the success almost of any small plain thing, there being so many to think and speak to any business, and they of so uncertain minds and interests and passions.

He did tell me, and so did Sir W. Batten, how [Sir Allen Brodericke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9461/) and [Sir Allen Apsly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6462/) did come drunk the other day into the House, and did both speak for half an hour together, and could not be either laughed, or pulled, or bid to sit down and hold their peace, to the great contempt of the King’s servants and cause; which I am grieved at with all my heart.

We were full in discourse of the sad state of our times, and the horrid shame brought on the King’s service by the just clamours of the poor seamen, and that we must be undone in a little time.

Home full of trouble on these considerations, and, among other things, I to my chamber, and there to ticket a good part of my books, in order to the numbering of them for my easy finding them to read as I have occasion.

So to supper and to bed, with my heart full of trouble.

# [Thursday 20 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/20/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning, and here among other things come [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), and I did get him to sign me a note for the 100 _l._ to pay for the [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/) he do present me with, which I am very glad of. At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where was [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) come, who is well again, and the most recovered in his countenance that ever I did see. Here dined with me also [Mrs. Batters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7788/), poor woman! now left a sad widow by the drowning of [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7787/) the other day. I pity her, and will do her what kindness I can; yet I observe something of ill-nature in myself more than should be, that I am colder towards her in my charity than I should be to one so painful as he and she have been and full of kindness to their power to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I. After dinner out with Balty, setting him down at the [Maypole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10656/) in [the Strand](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/245/), and then I to my [Lord Bellasses](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8186/), and there spoke with [Mr. Moone](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9606/) about some business, and so away home to my business at the office, and then home to supper and to bed, after having finished the putting of little papers upon my books to be numbered hereafter.

# [Friday 21 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/21/)

Lay long, and when up find [Mrs. Clerk](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9069/) of [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/) and her daughter [Daniel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/), their business among other things was a request her daughter was to make, so I took her into my chamber, and there it was to help [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9530/) to the command of a little new pleasure boat building, which I promised to assist in. And here I had opportunity ‘para baiser elle, and toucher ses mamailles’ … [so as to make mi mismo espender with great pleasure. – L&M] Then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there did a little business, and then to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) and did the like. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and spent all the afternoon in putting some things, pictures especially, in order, and pasting my [Lady Castlemayne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/) print on a frame, which I have made handsome, and is a fine piece. So to the office in the evening to marshall my papers of accounts presented to the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/), against any future occasion to recur to them, which I did do to my great content. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and did some [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) work, and so to bed.

# [Saturday 22 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/22/)

At the office all the morning, and there come news from [Hogg](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10657/) that [our shipp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10396/) hath brought in a Lubecker to [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/), likely to prove [prize](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/), of [deals](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4992/), which joys us. At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/), and I met at [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to examine our papers, and have great hopes to prove her prize, and Sir R. Ford I find a mighty [yare](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10658/) man in this business, making exceeding good observations from the papers on our behalf. Hereupon concluded what to write to Hogg and [Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7120/), which I did, and also with [Mr. Oviatt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10659/) (Sir R. Ford’s son, who is to be our solicitor), to fee some counsel in the [Admiralty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/297/), but none in town. So home again, and after writing letters by the post, I with all my clerks and [Carcasse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8833/) and [Whitfield](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6489/) to the [ticket](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4086/)-office, there to be informed in the method and disorder of the office, which I find infinite great, of infinite concernment to be mended, and did spend till 12 at night to my great satisfaction, it being a point of our office I was wholly unacquainted in. So with great content home and to bed.

# [Sunday 23 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/23/)

(Lord’s day). Up and alone [to church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and meeting [Nan Wright](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7909/) at the gate had opportunity to take two or three ‘baisers’, and so to church, where a vain fellow with a [periwigg](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/517/) preached, Chaplain, as by his prayer appeared, to the [Earl of Carlisle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11205/). [Home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there dined with us [Betty Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5329/) and [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9771/). After dinner to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) by coach, and took them with me. And in the way I would have taken ‘su main’ as I did the last time, but she did in a manner withhold it. So set them down at White Hall, and I to [the Chapel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1042/) to find [Dr. Gibbons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2612/), and from him to the [Harp and Ball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5782/) to transcribe the treble which I would have him to set a bass to. But this took me so much time, and it growing night, I was fearful of missing a coach, and therefore took a coach and to rights to call Michell and his wife at their father [Howlett’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6514/), and so home, it being cold, and the ground all snow … [but the moon shining. # [Monday 24 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/24/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/), [[Sir] J. Mennes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), [[Sir] W. Penn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), and myself met, and there I did use my notes I took on Saturday night about [tickets](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4086/), and did come to a good settlement in the business of that office, if it be kept to, this morning being a meeting on purpose. At noon to prevent my Lord Bruncker’s dining here I walked as if upon business with him, it being frost and dry, as far as [Paul’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/280/), and so back again through [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) by [Guildhall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/129/), observing the ruines thereabouts, till I did truly lose myself, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner. I do truly find that I have overwrought my eyes, so that now they are become weak and apt to be tired, and all excess of light makes them sore, so that now to the candlelight I am forced to sit by, adding, the snow upon the ground all day, my eyes are very bad, and will be worse if not helped, so my Lord Bruncker do advise as a certain cure to use greene [spectacles](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10635/), which I will do. So to dinner, where [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) with us, and very merry. After dinner she goes and fetches [a little son](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13624/) of [Mr. Backeworth’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8716/), the wittiest child and of the most spirit that ever I saw in my life for discourse of all kind, and so ready and to the purpose, not above four years old. Thence to [Sir Robert Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/), and there paid for the [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/) I have bought to the value of 94 _l._, with the 100 _l._[Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) did give me to that purpose, and received the rest in money. I this evening did buy me a pair of green spectacles, to see whether they will help my eyes or no. So to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and went to the Upper ’Change, which is almost as good as the old one; only shops are but on one side. Then home to the office, and did business till my eyes began to be bad, and so home to supper. My people busy making [mince pies](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3371/), and so to bed. No newes yet of our [Gottenburgh](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9624/) fleete; which makes [us] have some fears, it being of mighty concernment to have our supply of [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/) safe. I met with [Mr. Cade](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5737/) to-night, my stationer; and he tells me that he hears for certain that the [Queene-Mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1399/) is about and hath near finished a peace with France, which, as a [Presbyterian](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/447/), he do not like, but seems to fear it will be a means to introduce [Popery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/306/).

# [Tuesday 25 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/25/)

([Christmas day](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/)). Lay pretty long in bed, and then rose, leaving [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) desirous to sleep, having sat up till four this morning seeing her mayds make [mince-pies](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3371/). I to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where our parson [Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/) made a good sermon. Then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and dined well on some good ribbs of [beef](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/381/) roasted and mince pies; only my wife, [brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/117/), and [Barker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8981/), and plenty of good [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) of my owne, and my heart full of true joy; and thanks to God Almighty for the goodness of my condition at this day. After dinner, I begun to teach my wife and Barker my song, [“It is decreed,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10288/) which pleases me mightily as now I have [Mr. Hinxton’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10654/) base. Then out and walked alone on foot to the [Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/), it being a fine frost, thinking to have seen a play all alone; but there, missing of any bills, concluded there was none, and so back home; and there with my brother reducing the names of all my books to an alphabet, which kept us till 7 or 8 at night, and then to supper, [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) with us, and pretty merry, and then to my chamber to enter this day’s journal only, and then to bed. My head a little thoughtfull how to behave myself in the business of the [victualling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9960/), which I think will be prudence to offer my service in doing something in passing the pursers’ accounts, thereby to serve [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), get honour to myself, and confirm me in my place in the victualling, which at present yields not work enough to deserve [my wages](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9082/).

# [Wednesday 26 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/26/)

Up, and walked all the way (it being a most fine frost), to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), to [Sir W. Coventry’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) chamber, and thence with him up to the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), where among other things at our meeting I did offer my assistance to [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) to do the business of his office, relating to the Pursers’ accounts, which was well accepted by the Duke of York, and I think I have and shall do myself good in it, if it be taken, for it will confirm me in the business of the [victualling office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3221/), which I do now very little for. Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), carrying a barrel of [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/) with me. Anon comes [Mr. John Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9485/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9486/) by invitation from [Bow](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5228/) to dine with me, and young [Batelier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10670/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10671/) with her great belly, which has spoiled her looks mightily already. Here was also [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), whom I met coming home, who tells me of a most bitter lampoone now out against the Court and the management of State from head to foot, mighty witty and mighty severe. By and by to dinner, a very good one, and merry. After dinner I put the women into a coach, and they to the [Duke’s house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/), to a play which was acted, “The ————.” It was indifferently done, but was not pleased with the song, [Gosnell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5618/) not singing, but a new wench, that sings naughtily. Thence home, all by coach, and there Mr. Andrews to the [vyall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/461/), who plays most excellently on it, which I did not know before. Then to dance, here being [Pembleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6197/) come, by [my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) direction, and a fiddler; and we got, also, the elder [Batelier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10243/) to-night, and [Nan Wright](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7909/), and mighty merry we were, and I danced; and so till twelve at night, and to supper, and then to [cross purposes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10672/), mighty merry, and then to bed, my eyes being sore. Creed lay here in [Barker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8981/) bed.

# [Thursday 27 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/27/)

Up; and called up by [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/)[trumpets](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10492/), which cost me 10 _s._ So to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon, by invitation, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), who had not been there these 10 months, I think, and I, to meet all our families at [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) at dinner, whither neither a great dinner for so much company nor anything good or handsome. In the middle of dinner I rose, and my wife, and by coach to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), and meeting [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) took him up, and there saw [“The Scornfull Lady”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5636/) well acted; [Doll Common](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10673/) doing Abigail most excellently, and [Knipp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/) the widow very well, and will be an excellent actor, I think. In other parts the play not so well done as used to be, by the old actors. Anon to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) by coach, thinking to have seen a play there to-night, but found it a mistake, so back again, and missed our coach[man], who was gone, thinking to come time enough three hours hence, and we could not blame him. So forced to get another coach, and all three home to my house, and there to Sir W. Batten’s, and eat a bit of cold [chine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1705/) of [beef](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/381/), and then staid and talked, and then home and sat and talked a little by the fireside with my wife and Creed, and so to bed, my left eye being very sore. No business publick or private minded all these two days. This day a house or two was blown up with powder in the [Minorys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6103/), and several people spoiled, and many dug out from under the rubbish.

# [Friday 28 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/28/)

Up, and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) and I walked (a very fine walk in the frost) to my [Lord Bellasses](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8186/), but missing him did find him at [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there spoke with him about some [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) business. That done, we to Creed’s lodgings, which are very pretty, but he is going from them. So we to [Lincoln’s Inne Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), he to [Ned Pickering’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/612/), who it seems lives there, keeping a good house, and I to my [Lord Crew’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/105/), where I dined, and hear the newes how my Lord’s brother, [Mr. Nathaniel Crew](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4186/), hath an estate of 6 or 700 _l._ per annum, left him by the death of an old acquaintance of his, but not akin to him at all. And this man is dead without will, but had, above ten years since, made over his estate to this Mr. Crew, to him and his heirs for ever, and given Mr. Crew the keeping of the deeds in his own hand all this time; by which, if he would, he might have taken present possession of the estate, for he knew what they were. This is as great an act of confident friendship as this latter age, I believe, can shew. From hence to the [Duke’s house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/), and there saw [“Macbeth”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8004/) most excellently acted, and a most excellent play for variety. I had sent for [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) to meet me there, who did come, and after the play was done, I out so soon to meet her at the other door that I left my cloake in the playhouse, and while I returned to get it, she was gone out and missed me, and with [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) away home. I not sorry for it much did go to White Hall, and got my Lord Bellasses to get me into the playhouse; and there, after all staying above an hour for the players, [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and all waiting, which was absurd, saw [“Henry the Fifth”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7791/) well done by the Duke’s people, and in most excellent habits, all new [vests](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10449/), being put on but this night. But I sat so high and far off, that I missed most of the words, and sat with a wind coming into my back and neck, which did much trouble me.

The play continued till twelve at night; and then up, and a most horrid cold night it was, and frosty, and moonshine. But the worst was, I had left my cloak at [Sir G. Carteret’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/), and they being abed I was forced to go home without it. So by chance got a coach and to the [Golden Lion Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10675/) in [the Strand](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/245/), and there drank some mulled [sack](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), and so home, where find my poor wife staying for me, and then to bed mighty cold.

# [Saturday 29 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/29/)

Up, called up with newes from [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) that [Hogg](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10657/) hath brought in two [prizes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/) more: and so I thither, and hear the particulars, which are good; one of them, if prize, being worth 4,000 _l._: for which God be thanked! Then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and have the newes brought us of [Captain Robinson’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10676/) coming with his fleete from [Gottenburgh](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9624/): dispersed, though, by foul weather. But he hath light of five Dutch men-of-war, and taken three, whereof one is sunk; which is very good newes to close up the year with, and most of our merchantmen already heard of to be safely come home, though after long lookings-for, and now to several ports, as they could make them. At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) is and now well recovered. Then to the office to do business, and at night, it being very cold, home to my chamber, and there late writing, but my left eye still very sore. I write by [spectacles](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10635/) all this night, then to supper and to bed. This day’s good news making me very lively, only the arrears of much business on my hands and my accounts to be settled for the whole year past do lie as a weight on my mind.

# [Sunday 30 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/30/)

(Lord’s day). Lay long, however up and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where [Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/) made a good sermon. Here was a collection for [the sexton](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14114/); but it come into my head why we should be more bold in making the collection while the psalm is singing, than in the sermon or prayer. [Home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and, without any strangers, to dinner, and then all the afternoon and evening in my chamber preparing all my accounts in good condition against to-morrow, to state them for the whole year past, to which God give me a good issue when I come to close them!

So to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 31 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/31/)

Rising this day with a full design to mind nothing else but to make up my accounts for the year past, I did take money, and walk forth to several places in the towne as far as the [New Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1085/), to pay all my debts, it being still a very great frost and good walking. I staid at the [Fleece Tavern](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1642/) in [Covent Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/126/) while my boy [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/) went to [W. Joyce’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/) to pay what I owed for candles there. Thence to the New Exchange to clear [my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) score, and so going back again I met [Doll Lane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10215/) ([Mrs. Martin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/) sister), with another young woman of [the Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), one [Scott](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10694/), and took them to the [Half Moon Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/957/) and there drank some burnt [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) with them, without more pleasure, and so away [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) by coach, and there to dinner, and then to my accounts, wherein, at last, I find them clear and right; but, to my great discontent, do find that my gettings this year have been 573 _l._ less than my last: it being this year in all but 2,986 _l._; whereas, the last, I got 3,560 _l._. And then again my spendings this year have exceeded my spendings the last by 644 _l._: my whole spendings last year being but 509 _l._; whereas this year, it appears, I have spent 1154 _l._, which is a sum not fit to be said that ever I should spend in one year, before I am master of a better estate than I am. Yet, blessed be God! and I pray God make me thankful for it, I do find myself worth in money, all good, [above 6,200 _l._](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9548/); which is above 1800 _l._ more than I was the last year. This, I trust in God, will make me thankfull for what I have, and carefull to make up by care next year what by my negligence and prodigality I have lost and spent this year.

The doing of this, and entering of it fair, with the sorting of all my expenses, to see how and in what points I have exceeded, did make it late work, till my eyes become very sore and ill, and then did give over, and supper, and to bed.

Thus ends this year of publick wonder and mischief to this nation, and, therefore, generally wished by all people to have an end. Myself and family well, [having](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8981/)[four](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/)[mayds](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10106/)[and](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6687/) one clerk, Tom, in my house, and [my brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/117/), now with me, to spend time in order to his preferment. Our healths all well, only my eyes with overworking them are sore as candlelight comes to them, and not else; publick matters in a most sad condition; seamen discouraged for want of pay, and are become not to be governed: nor, as matters are now, can any fleete go out next year. Our enemies, French and Dutch, great, and grow more by our poverty. The [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) backward in raising, because jealous of the spending of the money; [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) less and less likely to be built again, every body settling elsewhere, and nobody encouraged to trade. A sad, vicious, negligent Court, and all sober men there fearful of the ruin of the whole kingdom this next year; from which, good God deliver us! One thing I reckon remarkable in my owne condition is, that I am come to abound in good [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/), so as at all entertainments to be served wholly with silver plates, having two dozen and a half.

# Diary entries from December 1664

# [Thursday 1 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/01/)

Up betimes and to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to a [Committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), and so straight [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and hard to my business at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till noon, then to dinner, and so to my office, and by and by we sat all the afternoon, then to my office again till past one in the morning, and so home to supper and to bed.

[Read 13 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/01/#annotations)

# [Friday 2 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/02/)

Lay long in bed. Then up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy all the morning. At [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) dined. After dinner with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) to the [Duke’s House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/), and there saw [“The Rivalls,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7862/) which I had seen before; but the play not good, nor anything but the good actings of [Betterton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2307/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4034/) and [Harris](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6533/).

Thence homeward, and the coach broke with us in [Lincoln’s Inn Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), and so walked to [Fleete Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/127/), and there took coach and home, and to my office, whither by and by comes [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), and then [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and we all to [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), and I did give them a barrel of [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/) I had given to me, and so there sat and talked, where good discourse of the late troubles, they knowing things, all of them, very well; and Cocke, from [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/624/) own mouth, being then entrusted himself much, do know particularly that the King’s credulity to [Cromwell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/796/) promises, private to him, against the advice of his friends and the certain discovery of the practices and discourses of Cromwell in council (by [Major Huntington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8076/)) did take away his life and nothing else.1

Then to some loose atheisticall discourse of Cocke’s, when he was almost drunk, and then about 11 o’clock broke up, and I to my office, to fit up an account for Povy, wherein I hope to get something. At it till almost two o’clock, then to supper and to bed.

1.   According to Clarendon the officer here alluded to was a major in Cromwell’s own regiment of horse, and employed by him to treat with Charles I. whilst at Hampton Court; but being convinced of the insincerity of the proceeding, communicated his suspicions to that monarch, and immediately gave up his commission. We hear no more of Huntington till the Restoration, when his name occurs with those of many other officers, who tendered their services to the king. His reasons for laying down his commission are printed in Thurloe’s “State Papers” and Maseres’s “Tracts.” — B. ↩

[Read 30 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/02/#annotations)

# [Saturday 3 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/)

Up, and at [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and at noon to [Mr. Cutler’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/), and there dined with [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/) and him, and thence Sir W. Rider and I by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to a Committee of [the Fishery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7696/); there only to hear [Sir Edward Ford’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6773/) proposal about farthings, wherein, O God! to see almost every body interested for him; only my [Lord Annesly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/887/), who is a grave, serious man. My [Lord Barkeley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/) was there, but is the most hot, fiery man in discourse, without any cause, that ever I saw, even to breach of civility to my Lord Anglesey, in his discourse opposing to my Lord’s. At last, though without much satisfaction to me, it was voted that it should be requested of [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and that Sir Edward Ford’s proposal is the best yet made. Thence by coach [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). The [Duke of Yorke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) being expected to-night with great joy from [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/), after his having been abroad at sea three or four days with the fleete; and the Dutch are all drawn into their harbours. But it seems like a victory: and a matter of some reputation to us it is, and blemish to them; but in no degree like what it is esteemed at, the weather requiring them to do so. Home and at my office late, and then to supper and to bed.

[Read 9 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/#annotations)

# [Sunday 4 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/04/)

(Lord’s day). Lay long in bed, and then up and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), there to dispatch a business in order to the getting something out of the [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) business, wherein I have an opportunity to get myself paid upon the score of freight. I hope a good sum.

At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then in the afternoon to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/). So home, and by and by comes [Mr. Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7165/) and [Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/), and sung together long and with great content. Then to supper and broke up. Pretty discourse, very pleasant and ingenious, and so to my office a little, and then home (after prayers) to bed.

This day I hear the [Duke of Yorke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) is come to towne, though expected last night, as I observed, but by what hindrance stopped I can’t tell.

[Read 27 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/04/#annotations)

# [Monday 5 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/05/)

Up, and to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) with [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/); and there, among an infinite crowd of great persons, did kiss [the Duke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) hand; but had no time to discourse. Thence up and down the gallery, and got my [Lord of Albemarle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) hand to my bill for [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), but afterwards was asked some scurvy questions by Povy about my demands, which troubled [me], but will do no great hurt I think. Thence vexed [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there by appointment comes my cozen [Roger Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/) and [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/), and dined with me, and very merry we were. They staid all the afternoon till night, and then after I had discoursed an hour with [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) plainly declaring my resolution to desert him if he goes on to join with [Castle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2461/), who and his family I, for great provocation, love not, which he takes with some trouble, but will concur in everything with me, he says. Now I am loth, I confess, to lose him, he having been the best friend I have had ever in this office. So he being gone, we all, it being night, in Madam Turner’s coach to her house, there to see, as she tells us, how fat [Mrs. The.](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/120/) is grown, and so I find her, but not as I expected, but mightily pleased I am to hear the mother commend her daughter [Betty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8086/) that she is like to be a great beauty, and she sets much by her.

Thence I to White Hall, and there saw [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) come to towne, and, with all my heart, am glad to see him, but could have no talke with him, he being but just come. Thence back and took up [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and home, where a while, and then home to supper and to bed.

# [Tuesday 6 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/06/)

Up, and in [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), but [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) being gone forth, I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and there spent much time till towards noon to and fro with people. So by and by [Mrs. Lane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/) comes and plucks me by the cloak to speak to me, and I was fain to go to her shop, and pretending to buy some [bands](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5633/) made her go home, and by and by followed her, and there did what I would with her, and so after many discourses and her intreating me to do something for [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/), which I promised to do, and buying a little band of her, which I intend to keep to, I took leave, there coming a couple of footboys to her with a coach to fetch her abroad I know not to whom. She is great with child, and she says I must be godfather, but I do not intend it. Thence by coach to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and there hear that the Dutch are fitting their ships out again, which puts us to new discourse, and to alter our thoughts of the Dutch, as to their want of courage or force. Thence by appointment to the [White Horse Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8054/) in [Lumbard Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/966/), and there dined with my [Lord Rutherford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5728/), [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), [Mr. Gauden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), and others, and very merry, and after dinner among other things Povy and I withdrew, and I plainly told him that I was concerned in profit, but very justly, in this business of the Bill that I have been these two or three days about, and he consents to it, and it shall be paid.

He tells me how he believes, and in part knows, Creed to be worth 10,000 _l._; nay, that now and then he [Povy] hath three or 4,000 _l._ in his hands, for which he gives the interest that [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) gives, which is ten per cent., and that Creed do come and demand it every three months the interest to be paid him, which Povy looks upon as a cunning and mean tricke of him; but for all that, he will do and is very rich. Thence to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat and where [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) came the first time after his return from sea, which I was glad of.

So after office to my office, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper, and to my office again, and then late home to bed.

# [Wednesday 7 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/07/)

Lay long, then up, and among others [Bagwell’s wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6480/) coming to speak with me put new thoughts of folly into me which I am troubled at. Thence after doing business at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), I by coach to my [Lady Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and there dined with her, and found all well and merry. Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and we waited on [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), who looks better than he did, methinks, before his voyage; and, I think, a little more stern than he used to do.

Thence to [the Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/) to my cozen [Roger Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/), thinking to have met the Doctor to have discoursed our business, but he came not, so I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there by agreement came my [Lord Rutherford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5728/), [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), [Gauden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), [Alderman Backewell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/967/), about [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) business of accounts between Rutherford and Gauden. Here they were with me an hour or more, then after drinking away, and Povy and Creed staid and eat with me; but I was sorry I had no better cheer for Povy; for the foole may be useful, and is a cunning fellow in his way, which is a strange one, and that, that I meet not in any other man, nor can describe in him. They late with me, and when gone [my boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/) and I to musique, and then to bed.

# [Thursday 8 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/08/)

Up, and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the morning busy. At noon dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and then to the office, where we sat all the afternoon. In the evening comes my [aunt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/995/) and [uncle Wight](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/911/), [Mrs. Norbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2725/), and her daughter, and after them [Mr. Norbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2724/), where no great pleasure, my aunt being out of humour in her fine clothes, and it raining hard. Besides, I was a little too bold with her about her doating on [Dr. Venner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8087/). Anon they went away, and I till past 12 at night at my office, and then home to bed.

# [Friday 9 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/09/)

Up betimes and walked to [Mr. Povy’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), and there, not without some few troublesome questions of his, I got a note, and went and received 117 _l._ 5 _s._ of [Alderman Viner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7169/) upon my pretended freight of the [“William”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8088/) for [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), which overbears me on one side with joy and on the other to think of my condition if I shall be called into examination about it, and (though in strictness it is due) not be able to give a good account of it.

[Home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) with it, and there comes [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) to me, and he and I did set even the business of the ship [Union](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8089/) lately gone for Tangier, wherein I hope to get 50 _l._ more, for all which the Lord be praised.

At noon home to dinner, [Mr. Hunt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/239/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/240/) with us, and very pleasant. Then in the afternoon I carried them home by coach, and I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and thence to [Gervas’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6230/), and there find I cannot prevail with [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7853/) to go forth with me, but though I took a good occasion of going to the [Trumpet](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1158/) she declined coming, which vexed me. ‘Je avait grande envie envers elle, avec vrai amour et passion’.

Thence home and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till one in the morning, setting to rights in writing this day’s two accounts of Povy and Taylor, and then quietly to bed.

This day I had several letters from several places, of our bringing in great numbers of Dutch ships.

# [Saturday 10 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/10/)

Lay long, at which I am ashamed, because of so many people observing it that know not how late I sit up, and for fear of [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) speaking of it to others, he having staid for me a good while. At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, where comes my [Lord Brunkard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) with his patent in his hand, and delivered it to [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and myself, we alone being there all the day, and at noon I in his coach with him to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), where he set me down; a modest civil person he seems to be, but wholly ignorant in the business of the Navy as possible, but I hope to make a friend of him, being a worthy man.

Thence after hearing the great newes of so many Dutchmen being brought in to [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/) and elsewhere, which it is expected will either put them upon present revenge or despair, I with [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/) and [Cutler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/) to dinner all alone to the [Great James](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2190/), where good discourse, and, I hope, occasion of getting something hereafter.

After dinner to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to the [Fishery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7696/), where [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) was with us.

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and late at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), writing many letters, then home to supper and to bed. Yesterday come home, and this night I visited [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), who dissembles great respect and love to me, but I understand him very well.

[Major Holmes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/930/) is come from [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/), and is now at [Plymouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5849/) with great wealth, they say.

# [Sunday 11 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/11/)

(Lord’s day). Up and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) alone in the morning. Dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), mighty pleasantly. In the afternoon I to the [French church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5696/), where much pleased with the three sisters of [the parson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8090/), very handsome, especially in their noses, and sing prettily. I heard a good sermon of [the old man](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5747/), touching duty to parents. Here was [Sir Samuel Morland](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/779/) and [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8091/) very fine, with two footmen in new liverys (the church taking much notice of them), and going into their coach after sermon with great gazeing. So I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and my cozen, [Mary Pepys’s husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6750/), comes after me, and told me that out of the money he received some months since he did receive 18 _d._ too much, and did now come and give it me, which was very pretty. So home, and there found [Mr. Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/) and [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8645/), a well-bred and a tolerable pretty woman, and by and by [Mr. Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7165/) and to singing, and then to supper, then to sing again, and so good night. To prayers and tonight [bed].

It is a little strange how these [Psalms](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8056/) of [Ravenscroft](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8055/) after 2 or 3 times singing prove but the same again, though good. No diversity appearing at all almost.

# [Monday 12 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/12/)

Up, and with [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where all of us with [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/); [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) privately did tell me the reason of his advice against our pretences to the [Prize Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8052/) (in his letter from Portsmouth), because he knew that the King and the Duke had resolved to put in some Parliament men that have deserved well, and that would needs be obliged, by putting them in.

Thence homeward, called at [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) and bespoke some books against the year’s out, and then to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where my [Lord Brunkard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) comes and reads over part of our Instructions in the Navy — and I expounded it to him, so he is become my disciple. He gone, comes [Cutler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/) to tell us that the [King of France](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/) hath forbid any canvass to be carried out of his kingdom, and I to examine went with him to the [East India house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2492/) to see a letter, but came too late. So home again, and there late till 12 at night at my office, and then home to supper and to bed.

This day (to see how things are ordered in the world), I had a command from the [Earle of Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), at [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/), not to be forward with [Mr. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/) and [Sir J. Lawson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/110/) about the [Mole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5384/) at [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), because that what I do therein will (because of his friendship to me known) redound against him, as if I had done it upon his score. So I wrote to my Lord my mistake, and am contented to promise never to pursue it more, which goes against my mind with all my heart.

# [Tuesday 13 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/13/)

Lay long in bed, then up, and many people to speak with me. Then to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and dined at noon at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), then to the office again, where we sat all the afternoon, and then home at night to a little supper, and so after my office again at 12 at night home to bed.

# [Wednesday 14 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/14/)

Up, and after a while at [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), I abroad in several places, among others to [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/), and there spoke for several books against New Year’s day, I resolving to lay out about 7 _l._ or 8 _l._, God having given me some profit extraordinary of late; and bespoke also some [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/), spoons, and forks. I pray God keep me from too great expenses, though these will still be pretty good money. Then to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) and [Mr. Caesar](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8104/), [my boy’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/)[lute](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/540/) master, who plays indeed mighty finely, and after dinner I abroad, parting from Creed, and away to and fro, laying out or preparing for laying out more money, but I hope and resolve not to exceed therein, and to-night spoke for some fruit for the country for [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) against [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), and where should I do it, but at the pretty woman’s, that used to stand at the doore in [Fanchurch Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1075/), I having a mind to know her.

So home, and late at my office, evening reckonings with [Shergoll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8105/), hoping to get money by the business, and so away home to supper and to bed, not being very well through my taking cold of late, and so troubled with some wind.

# [Thursday 15 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)

Called up very betimes by [Mr. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), and with him a good while about some of his [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts; and, discoursing of the condition of Tangier, he did give me the whole account of the differences between [Fitzgerald](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5385/) and [Norwood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/678/), which were very high on both sides, but most imperious and base on Fitzgerald’s, and yet through my [Lord FitzHarding’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1686/) means, the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) is led rather to blame Norwood and to speake that he should be called home, than be sensible of the other. He is a creature of FitzHarding’s, as a fellow that may be done with what he will, and, himself certainly pretending to be Generall of the King’s armies, when [Monk](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) dyeth, desires to have as few great or wise men in employment as he can now, but such as he can put in and keep under, which he do this coxcomb Fitzgerald.

It seems, of all mankind there is no man so led by another as the Duke is by [Lord Muskerry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7614/) and this FitzHarding. Insomuch, as when the King would have him to be Privy-Purse, the Duke wept, and said, “But, Sir, I must have your promise, if you will have my dear Charles from me, that if ever you have occasion for an army again, I may have him with me; believing him to be the best commander of an army in the world.” But Mr. Cholmly thinks, as all other men I meet with do, that he is a very ordinary fellow.

It is strange how the Duke also do love naturally, and affect the Irish above the English. He, of the company he carried with him to sea, took above two-thirds Irish and French.

He tells me [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) do hate my [Lord Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/); and that they, that is the King and my Lord FitzHarding, do laugh at him for a dull fellow; and in all this business of the Dutch war do nothing by his advice, hardly consulting him. Only he is a good minister in other respects, and the King cannot be without him; but, above all, being the Duke’s father-in-law, he is kept in; otherwise FitzHarding were able to fling down two of him. This, all the wise and grave lords see, and cannot help it; but yield to it.

But he bemoans what the end of it may be, the King being ruled by these men, as he hath been all along since his coming; to the razing all the strong-holds in Scotland, and giving liberty to the Irish in Ireland, whom [Cromwell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/796/) had settled all in one corner; who are now able, and it is feared everyday a massacre again among them.

He being gone I abroad to the carrier’s, to see some things sent away to [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) against [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), and thence to [Moorfields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2188/), and there up and down to several houses to drink to look for a place ‘pour rencontrer la femme de je sais quoi’ against next Monday, but could meet none. So to the [Coffeehouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/813/), where great talke of the Comet seen in several places; and among our men at sea, and by my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), to whom I intend to write about it to-night.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the afternoon, and in the evening home to supper, and then to the office late, and so to bed.

This night I begun to burn wax candles in my closett at the office, to try the charge, and to see whether the smoke offends like that of tallow candles.

# [Friday 16 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/16/)

Up, and by water to [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/), thinking to have met [‘la femme de’ Bagwell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6480/), but failed, and having done some business at the yard, I back again, it being a fine fresh morning to walk. Back again, [Mr. Wayth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1313/) walking with me to [Half-Way House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4210/) talking about [Mr. Castle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2461/) fine [knees](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6807/) lately delivered in. In which I am well informed that they are not as they should be to make them knees, and I hope shall make good use of it to [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) service.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and having dressed myself, to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and thence home to dinner, and so abroad by coach with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and bought a looking glasse by the Old Exchange, which costs me 5 _l._ 5 _s._ and 6 _s._ for the hooks. A very fair glasse.

So toward my cozen [Scott’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1761/), but meeting my [Lady Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) coach, my wife turned back to follow them, thinking they might, as they did, go to visit her, and I ’light and to [Mrs. Harman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6626/), and there staid and talked in her shop with her, and much pleased I am with her. We talked about [Anthony Joyce’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) giving over trade and that he intends to live in lodgings, which is a very mad, foolish thing. She tells me she hears and believes it is because he, being now begun to be called on offices, resolves not to take the new oathe, he having formerly taken the Covenant or Engagement, but I think he do very simply and will endeavour for [his wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/) sake to advise him therein.

Thence to my cozen Scott’s, and there met my cozen [Roger Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/), and [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/), and [The.](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/120/) and [Joyce](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/935/), and prated all the while, and so with the “corps” to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5185/) and heard a very fine sermon of [the Parson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8106/) of the parish, and so homeward with them in their coach, but finding it too late to go home with me, I took another coach and so home, and after a while at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), home to supper and to bed.

# [Saturday 17 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/17/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon I to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and there, among others, had my first meeting with [Mr. L’Estrange](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6713/), who hath endeavoured several times to speak with me. It is to get, now and then, some newes of me, which I shall, as I see cause, give him. He is a man of fine conversation, I think, but I am sure most courtly and full of compliments.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then come the looking-glass man to set up the looking-glass I bought yesterday, in my dining-room, and very handsome it is.

So abroad by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there to the [Committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), and then the [Fishing](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7696/).

[Mr. Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/) did in discourse give me a rub about my late bill for money that I did get of him, which vexed me and stuck in my mind all this evening, though I know very well how to cleare myself at the worst.

So home and to my office, where late, and then home to bed.

Mighty talke there is of this Comet that is seen a’nights; and [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and [Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) did sit up last night to see it, and did, it seems. And to-night I thought to have done so too; but it is cloudy, and so no stars appear. But I will endeavour it.

[Mr. Gray](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7821/) did tell me to-night, for certain, that the Dutch, as high as they seem, do begin to buckle; and that one man in this Kingdom did tell the King that he is offered 40,000 _l._ to make a peace, and others have been offered money also. It seems the taking of their [Bourdeaux](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8802/) fleete thus, arose from a printed Gazette of the Dutch’s boasting of fighting, and having beaten the English: in confidence whereof (it coming to Bourdeaux), all the fleete comes out, and so falls into our hands.
