# [Friday 23 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/23/)

Up and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), then come by appointment cozen [Tom Trice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2784/) to me, and I paid him the 20 _l._ remaining due to him upon the bond of 100 _l._ given him by agreement [November, 1663](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/11/17/), to end the difference between us about my aunt’s, his mother’s, money. And here, being willing to know the worst, I told him, “I hope now there is nothing remaining between you and I of future dispute.” “No,” says he, “nothing at all that I know of, but only a small matter of about 20 or 30 _s._ that [my father Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/884/) received for me of rent due to me in the country, which I will in a day or two bring you an account of,” and so we parted.

Dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) upon a good [turkey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/378/) which [Mr. Sheply](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) sent us, then to the office all the afternoon.

[Mr. Cutler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/) and others coming to me about business. I hear that the Dutch have prepared a fleete to go the backway to the [Streights](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3260/), where without doubt they will master our fleete. This put to that of [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/) makes me fear them mightily, and certainly they are a most wise people, and careful of their business. The [King of France](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/), they say, do declare himself obliged to defend them, and lays claim by his Embassador to the wines we have taken from the Dutch Bourdeaux men, and more, it is doubted whether the Swede will be our friend or no. Pray God deliver us out of these troubles!

This day [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) sent and afterwards spoke to me, to have me and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) come and dine with them on Monday next: which is a mighty condescension in them, and for some great reason I am sure, or else it pleases God by my late care of business to make me more considerable even with them than I am sure they would willingly owne me to be. God make me thankfull and carefull to preserve myself so, for I am sure they hate me and it is hope or fear that makes them flatter me.

It being a bright night, which it has not been a great while, I purpose to endeavour to be called in the morning to see the Comet, though I fear we shall not see it, because it rises in the east but 16 degrees, and then the houses will hinder us.

# [Saturday 24 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/24/)

Having sat up all night to past two o’clock this morning, our porter, being appointed, comes and tells us that the bellman tells him that the star is seen upon [Tower Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1395/); so I, that had been all night setting in order all my old papers in my chamber, did leave off all, and my boy and I to Tower Hill, it being a most fine, bright moonshine night, and a great frost; but no Comet to be seen. So after running once round the Hill, I and [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/), we [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and then to bed.

Rose about 9 o’clock and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where sitting all the morning. At noon to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), to the [Coffee-house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7944/); and there heard [Sir Richard Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/) tell the whole story of our defeat at [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/). Wherein our men are guilty of the most horrid cowardice and perfidiousness, as he says and tells it, that ever Englishmen were. [Captain Raynolds](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8124/), that was the only commander of any of the King’s ships there, was shot at by [De Ruyter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7463/), with a bloody flag flying. He, instead of opposing (which, indeed, had been to no purpose, but only to maintain honour), did poorly go on board himself, to ask what De Ruyter would have; and so yielded to whatever Ruyter would desire. [The King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and [Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) are highly vexed at it, it seems, and the business deserves it.

Thence home to dinner, and then abroad to buy some things, and among others to [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/), and there saw several books I spoke for, which are finely bound and good books to my great content.

So home and to my office, where late. This evening I being informed did look and saw the Comet, which is now, whether worn away or no I know not, but appears not with a tail, but only is larger and duller than any other star, and is come to rise betimes, and to make a great arch, and is gone quite to a new place in the heavens than it was before: but I hope in a clearer night something more will be seen. So home to bed.

# [Sunday 25 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/25/)

(Lord’s day and [Christmas day](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/)). Up ([my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) eye being ill still of the blow I did in a passion give her on [Monday last](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/)) to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) alone, where [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/), a good sermon. To dinner at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), where very pleasant with my wife and family. After dinner I to [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and there received so much good usage (as I have of late done) from him and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/), obliging me and my wife, according to promise, to come and dine with them to-morrow with our neighbours, that I was in pain all the day, and night too after, to know how to order the business of my wife’s not going, and by discourse receive fresh instances of [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) folly in complaining to [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) of Sir W. Batten and me for some family offences, such as my having of a stopcock to keepe the water from them, which vexes me, but it would more but that Sir G. Carteret knows him very well. Thence to the French church, but coming too late I returned and to [Mr. Rawlinson’s church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8125/), where I heard a good sermon of one that I remember was at [Paul’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1597/) with me, his name [Maggett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8126/); and very great store of fine women there is in this church, more than I know anywhere else about us.

So home and to my chamber, looking over and setting in order my papers and books, and so to supper, and then to prayers and to bed.

# [Monday 26 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/26/)

Up, and with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there with the rest did our usual business before [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), and then with [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) back and to his house, where I by sicknesse excused [my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) coming to them to-day. Thence I to the [Coffeehouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/813/), where much good discourse, and all the opinion now is that the Dutch will avoid fighting with us at home, but do all the hurte they can to us abroad; which it may be they may for a while, but that, I think, cannot support them long.

Thence to Sir W. Batten’s, where [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) and all our families here, women and all, and [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/) and his, and a great feast and good discourse and merry, there all the afternoon and evening till late, only stepped in to see my wife, then to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) to enter my day’s work, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to bed, where my people and wife innocently at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) very merry, and I to bed, leaving them to their sport and [blindman’s buff](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8155/).

[Read 24 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/26/#annotations)

# [Tuesday 27 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/27/)

My people came to bed, after their sporting, at four o’clock in the morning; I up at seven, and to [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/) and [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/) in a [gally](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7865/); [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) calling to me out of the barge in which [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) was with him going down the river, to know whither I was going. I told him to Woolwich, but was troubled afterward I should say no farther, being in a gally, lest he think me too profuse in my journeys.

Did several businesses, and then back again by two o’clock to [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) to dinner by appointment, where all yesterday’s company but [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), who could not come. Here merry, and after an hour’s chat I down to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy late, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper and to bed. The Comet appeared again to-night, but duskishly.

I went to bed, leaving [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and all her folks, and [Will](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) also, too, come to make [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) gambolls to-night.

[Read 23 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/27/#annotations)

# [Wednesday 28 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/28/)

I waked in the morning about 6 o’clock and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) not come to bed; I lacked a pot, but there was none, and bitter cold, so was forced to rise and piss in the chimney, and to bed again. Slept a little longer, and then hear my people coming up, and so I rose, and my wife to bed at eight o’clock in the morning, which vexed me a little, but I believe there was no hurt in it all, but only mirthe, therefore took no notice.

I abroad with [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to the Council Chamber, where all of us to discourse about the way of measuring ships and the freight fit to give for them by the tun, where it was strange methought to hear so poor discourses among the Lords themselves, and most of all to see how a little empty matter delivered gravely by [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) was taken mighty well, though nothing in the earth to the purpose. But clothes, I perceive more and more every day, is a great matter. Thence home with Sir W. Batten by coach, and I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, finding my wife still in bed. After dinner abroad, and among other things visited my [Lady Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and was there, with her and the young ladies, playing at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) till night. Then home and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) late, then home to bed, leaving my wife and people up to more sports, but without any great satisfaction to myself therein.

# [Thursday 29 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/29/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. Then whereas I should have gone and dined with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) (and the rest of [the officers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1121/) at his house), I pretended to dine with my [Lady Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), where I dined well, and began to wipe and clean my books in my chamber in order to the settling of my papers and things there thoroughly, and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the afternoon sitting, and in the evening home to supper, and then to my work again.

[Read 24 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/29/#annotations)

# [Friday 30 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/30/)

Lay very long in bed with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), it being very cold, and my wife very full of a resolution to keepe within doors, not so much as to go to church or see my [Lady Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) before [Easter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/315/) next, which I am willing enough to, though I seem the contrary. This and other talke kept me a-bed till almost 10 a’clock. Then up and made an end of looking over all my papers and books and taking everything out of my chamber to have all made clean. At noon dined, and after dinner forth to several places to pay away money, to clear myself in all the world, and, among others, paid [my bookseller](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) 6 _l._ for books I had from him this day, and the silversmith 22 _l._ 18 _s._ for spoons, forks, and sugar box, and being well pleased with seeing my business done to my mind as to my meeting with people and having my books ready for me, I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there did business late, and then home to supper, prayers, and to bed.

# [Saturday 31 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/31/)

At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and after dinner there again, dispatched first my letters, and then to my accounts, not of the month but of the whole yeare also, and was at it till past twelve at night, it being bitter cold; but yet I was well satisfied with my worke, and, above all, to find myself, by the great blessing of God, [worth 1349 _l._](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9548/), by which, as I have spent very largely, so I have laid up above 500 _l._ this yeare above what I was worth this day twelvemonth. The Lord make me for ever thankful to his holy name for it!

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to eat a little and so to bed. Soon as ever the clock struck one, I kissed [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in the kitchen by the fireside, wishing her a merry new yeare, observing that I believe I was the first proper wisher of it this year, for I did it as soon as ever the clock struck one.

So ends the old yeare, I bless God, with great joy to me, not only from my having made so good a yeare of profit, as having spent 420 _l._ and laid up 540 _l._ and upwards.

But I bless God I never have been in so good plight as to my health in so very cold weather as this is, nor indeed in any hot weather, these ten years, as I am at this day, and have been these four or five months. But I am at a great losse to know whether it be my hare’s foote, or taking every morning of a pill of [turpentine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7123/), or my having left off the wearing of a gowne.

My family is, my wife, in good health, and happy with her; her woman [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/), a pretty, modest, quiett mayde; her chambermayde [Besse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6788/), her cook mayde [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7583/), the little girl [Susan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6687/), and my boy, which I have had about half a yeare, [Tom Edwards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/), which I took from the King’s chappell, and a pretty and loving quiett family I have as any man in England.

My credit in the world and my office grows daily, and I am in good esteeme with everybody, I think.

My troubles of [my uncle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/884/)[estate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3384/) pretty well over; but it comes to be but of little profit to us, [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) being much supported by my purse.

But great vexations remain upon my father and me from my brother [Tom’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) death and ill condition, both to our disgrace and discontent, though no great reason for either.

Publique matters are all in a hurry about a Dutch warr. Our preparations great; our provocations against them great; and, after all our presumption, we are now afeard as much of them, as we lately contemned them.

Every thing else in the State quiett, blessed be God! My [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) at sea with the fleete at [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/); sending some about to cruise for taking of ships, which we have done to a great number.

This [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) I judged it fit to look over all my papers and books; and to tear all that I found either boyish or not to be worth keeping, or fit to be seen, if it should please God to take me away suddenly. Among others, I found these two or three notes, which I thought fit to keep.

Age of my Grandfather’s Children

Thomas,1595.
Mary,March 16, 1597.
Edith,October 11, 1599.
John, (my Father,)January 14, 1601.

My father and mother marryed at Newington, in Surry, Oct, 15, 1626

Theyr Children’s ages.

Mary,July 24, 1627.mort.1
Paulina Sept. 18, 1628.mort.
Esther,March 27, 1630.mort.
John,January 16, 1631.mort.
Samuel,Feb. 23, 1632.2
Thomas,June 18, 1634.mort.
Sarah,August 25, 1635.mort.
Jacob,May 1, 1637.mort.
Robert,Nov. 18, 1638.mort.
Paulina,Oct. 18, 1640.
John,Nov. 26, 1641.mort.

December 31, 1664.

Charmes for

1. Stenching of Blood.

Sanguis mane in te,  
 Sicut Christus fuit in se;  
 Sanguis mane in tua vena  
 Sicut Christus in sua poena;  
 Sanguis mane fixus,  
 Sicut Christus quando fuit crucifixus,

2. A Thorne.

Jesus, that was of a Virgin born,  
 Was pricked both with nail and thorn;  
 It neither wealed nor belled, rankled nor boned  
 In the name of Jesus no more shall this.

Or, thus:–

Christ was of a Virgin born;  
 And he was pricked with a thorn;  
 And it did neither bell, nor swell,  
 And I trust in Jesus this never will.

3. A Cramp.

Cramp be thou faintless,  
 As our Lady was sinless,  
 When she bare Jesus.

4. A Burning.

There came three Angells out of the East;  
 The one brought fire, the other brought frost—  
 Out fire; in frost.

In the name of the Father and Son, and Holy Ghost. Amen.

Wren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8019/), [Major Cooper](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9751/), and myself, mighty merry and pretty discourse."], [144, "Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat. Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/), being twelve plates more, and something else I have to choose. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) dined with me, and showed me a [Gazette](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9931/), in April last, which I wonder should never be remembered by any body, which tells how several persons were then tried for their lives, and were found guilty of a design of killing [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and destroying the Government; and as a means to it, to burn [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/); and that the day intended for the plot was the 3rd of last September.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/#fn1-1666-12-13) And [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) did indeed break out on the [2nd of September,](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/09/02/) which is very strange, methinks, and I shall remember it."], [180, "Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) newly come to town, from his being at [Chatham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/643/) and [Harwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7985/) to spy enormities: and at noon I with him and his lady [Williams](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8925/), to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), where a good dinner, and very merry. Good news to-day upon [the Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), that our [Hamburgh](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7009/) fleete is got in; and good hopes that we may soon have the like of our [Gottenburgh](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9624/), and then we shall be well for this winter. But then it shews them fools, that they would not permit this to have been done six weeks ago, which they might have had. At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where was [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) come, who is well again, and the most recovered in his countenance that ever I did see. Here dined with me also [Mrs. Batters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7788/), poor woman! now left a sad widow by the drowning of [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7787/) the other day. I pity her, and will do her what kindness I can; yet I observe something of ill-nature in myself more than should be, that I am colder towards her in my charity than I should be to one so painful as he and she have been and full of kindness to their power to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I. Mennes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), [[Sir] W. Penn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), and myself met, and there I did use my notes I took on Saturday night about [tickets](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4086/), and did come to a good settlement in the business of that office, if it be kept to, this morning being a meeting on purpose. So to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and went to the Upper ’Change, which is almost as good as the old one; only shops are but on one side. Then home to the office, and did business till my eyes began to be bad, and so home to supper. My people busy making [mince pies](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3371/), and so to bed. However, there I sat, near [Mr. Laneare](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9388/), with whom I spoke, and in sight, by chance, and very near my fat brown beauty of our Parish, the rich merchant’s lady, [a very noble woman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9470/), and [Madame Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/). A good sermon of [Mr. Plume’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8963/), and so to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), and there dined with him, and [Colonell Wyndham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9423/), a worthy gentleman, [whose wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9467/) was nurse to [the present King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and one that while she lived governed him and every thing else, as Cocke says, as a minister of state; [the old King](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/624/) putting mighty weight and trust upon her. They talked much of matters of State and persons, and particularly how my [Lord Barkeley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/) hath all along been a fortunate, though a passionate and but weak man as to policy; but as a kinsman brought in and promoted by my [Lord of St. Alban’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1618/), and one that is the greatest vapourer in the world, this Colonell Wyndham says; and one to whom only, with [Jacke Asheburnel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9471/) and [Colonel Legg](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7894/), the King’s removal to the [Isle of Wight](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6947/) from [Hampton Court](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1765/) was communicated; and (though betrayed by their knavery, or at best by their ignorance, insomuch that they have all solemnly charged one another with their failures therein, and have been at daggers-drawing publickly about it), yet now none greater friends in the world."], [64, "Several people to me about business, among others [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7624/), intended Storekeeper for [Harwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7985/), whom I did give some assistance in his dispatch by lending him money. So out and by water to London and to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and up and down about several businesses, and after the observing (God forgive me!) one or two of my neighbour Jason’s women [L&M have this as “my neighbour hermosa mohers”. Here was [her brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) come to see her, and speake with me about business. So to the ’Change. Up and down again in the evening about business and to meet [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), who waited for [Mrs. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) (with whom he is mightily stricken), to receive and hide for her her rich goods she saved the other day from seizure. So late by water home, taking a barrel of [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/) with me, and at [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/) went and sat with [Madam Penington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9050/) … [con laquelle je faisais almost whatever je voudrais — con mi mano, sino tocar la chose même; and I was very near it, – L&M] and made her undress her head and sit dishevilled all night sporting till two in the morning, and so away to [my lodging](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) and so to bed. Over-fasting all the morning hath filled me mightily with wind, and nothing else hath done it, that I fear a fit of the cholique."], [138, "Up betimes and finished my journall for five days back, and then after being ready to my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) by appointment, there to order the disposing of some money that we have come into the office, and here to my great content I did get a bill of imprest to [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) to pay myself in part of what is coming to me from him for my [Lord Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) satisfaction and my owne, and also another payment or two wherein I am concerned, and having done that did go to [Mr. Pierce’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/689/), where he and his wife made me drink some [tea](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/360/), and so he and I by water together to London. Here at a taverne in [Cornhill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1608/) he and I did agree upon my delivering up to him a bill of Captain Cocke’s, put into my hand for Pierce’s use upon evening of reckonings about the [prize goods](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/), and so away to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and there hear the ill news, to my great and all our great trouble, that [the plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/) is encreased again this week, notwithstanding there hath been a day or two great frosts; but we hope it is only the effects of the late close warm weather, and if the frosts continue the next week, may fall again; but the town do thicken so much with people, that it is much if the plague do not grow again upon us. Off the ’Change invited by [Sheriff Hooker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8904/), who keeps the poorest, mean, dirty table in a dirty house that ever I did see any [Sheriff of London](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11773/); and a plain, ordinary, silly man I think he is, but rich; only his son, [Mr. Lethulier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9500/), I like, for a pretty, civil, understanding merchant; and the more by much, because he happens to be husband to our noble, fat, brave [lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9470/) in our parish, that I and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) admire so. Thence away to the [Pope’s Head Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9544/), and there met first with [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), and dispatched my business with him to my content, he being ready to sign his bill of imprest of 2,000 _l._, and gives it me in part of his payment to me, which glads my heart. He being gone, comes [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/), who advised with me about several things about getting money, and 100 _l._ I shall presently have of him. We advised about a business of insurance, wherein something may be saved to him and got to me, and to that end he and I did take a coach at night and to the [Cockepitt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/179/), there to get the [Duke of Albemarle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) advice for our insuring some of our [Sounde](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9501/) goods coming home under [Harman’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8721/) convoy, but he proved shy of doing it without knowledge of the [Duke of Yorke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), so we back again and calling at my house to see my wife, who is well; though my great trouble is that our poor little parish is the greatest number this weeke in all the city within the walls, having six, from one the last weeke; and so by water to [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/) leaving Sir W. Warren at home, and I straight to my Lord Bruncker, it being late, and concluded upon insuring something and to send to that purpose to Sir W. Warren to come to us to-morrow morning. So I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) and, my mind in great rest, to bed."], [144, "Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) a while with my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/), where we directed [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) in the business of the insurance as I desired, and ended some other businesses of his, and so at noon I to London, but [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) was done before I got thither, so I to the [Pope’s Head Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9544/), and there find [Mr. Gawden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/) and [Captain Beckford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9048/) and [Nick Osborne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/991/) going to dinner, and I dined with them and very exceeding merry we were as I had [not] been a great while, and dinner being done I to the [East India House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2492/) and there had an assignment on [Mr. Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9022/) for the 2,000 _l._ of [Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), which joyed my heart; so, having seen [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in the way, I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) by water and to write my letters and then home to bed."], [182, "Up, and was trimmed, but not time enough to save my [Lord Bruncker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) coach or [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), and so was fain to walk to [Lambeth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1265/) on foot, but it was a very fine frosty walke, and great pleasure in it, but troublesome getting over [the River](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/) for ice. I to the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), whither my brethren were all come, but I was not too late. There we sat in discourse upon our Navy business an houre, and thence in my Lord Bruncker’s coach alone, he walking before (while I staid awhile talking with [Sir G. Downing](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/106/) about the Act, in which he is horrid troublesome) to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/). Thence I took [Sir Ellis Layton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7163/) to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), where my Lord Bruncker and [Lady Williams](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8925/) dine, and we all mighty merry; but Sir Ellis Layton one of the best companions at a meale in the world. After dinner I to [the Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) to see whether [my pretty seamstress](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8438/) be come again or no, and I find she is, so I to her, saluted her over her counter in the open Exchange above, and mightily joyed to see her, poor pretty woman! I must confess I think her a great beauty. After laying out a little money there for two pair of thread stockings, cost 8 _s._, I to [Lumbard Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/966/) to see some business to-night there at the goldsmith’s, among others paying in 1258 _l._ to [Viner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) for my [Lord Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) use upon Cocke’s account. I was called by my Lord Bruncker in his coach with his mistresse, and [Mr. Cottle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9529/) the lawyer, our acquaintance at [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to Greenwich, and thence I to [Mrs. Penington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9050/), and had a supper from the [King’s Head](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9015/) for her, and there mighty merry and free as I used to be with her, and at last, late, I did pray her to undress herself into her nightgowne, that I might see how to have her picture drawne carelessly (for she is mighty proud of that conceit), and I would walk without in the streete till she had done. So I did walk forth, and whether I made too many turns or no in the darke cold frosty night between the two walls up to the Parke gate I know not, but she was gone to bed when I come again to the house, upon pretence of leaving some papers there, which I did on purpose by her consent. So I away home, and was there sat up for to be spoken with my young [Mrs. Daniel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/), to pray me to speake for [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9530/) to be a Lieutenant. I had the opportunity here of kissing her again and again, and did answer that I would be very willing to do him any kindnesse, and so parted, and I to bed, exceedingly pleased in all my matters of money this month or two, it having pleased God to bless me with several opportunities of good sums, and that I have them in effect all very well paid, or in my power to have. But two things trouble me; one, [the sicknesse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/) is increased above 80 this weeke (though in my owne parish not one has died, though six the last weeke); the other, most of all, which is, that I have so complexed an account for these last two months for variety of layings out upon [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), occasions and variety of gettings that I have not made even with myself now these 3 or 4 months, which do trouble me mightily, finding that I shall hardly ever come to understand them thoroughly again, as I used to do my accounts when I was at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/)."], [188, "At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/) all the morning. At noon all of us dined at [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) at a good [chine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1705/) of [beef](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/381/), and other good meat; but, being all frost-bitten, was most of it unroast; but very merry, and a good dish of fowle we dressed ourselves. [Mr. Evelyn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1033/) there, in very good humour. All the afternoon till night pleasant, and then I took my leave of them and to the office, where I wrote my letters, and away [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/), my head full of business and some trouble for my letting my accounts go so far that I have made an oathe this night for the drinking no [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), &c., on such penalties till I have passed my accounts and cleared all. Coming home and going to bed, the boy tells me his sister [Daniel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/) has provided me a supper of little birds killed by [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9530/), and I made her sup with me, and after supper were alone a great while, and I had the pleasure of her lips, she being a pretty woman, and one whom a great belly becomes as well as ever I saw any. She gone, I to bed. This day I was come to by [Mrs. Burrows](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/), of Westminster, [Lieutenant Burrows](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9531/) (lately dead) [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/), a most pretty woman and my old acquaintance; I had a kiss or two of her, and a most modest woman she is."], [224, "Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), where [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and I met, to give our directions to the Commanders of all the ships in [the river](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/) to bring in lists of their ships’ companies, with entries, discharges, &c., all the last voyage, where young [Seymour](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9550/), among 20 that stood bare, stood with his hat on, a proud, saucy young man. Thence with them to [Mr. Cuttle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9529/), being invited, and dined nobly and neatly; with a very pretty house and a fine turret at top, with winding stairs and the finest prospect I know about all [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/), save the top of the hill, and yet in some respects better than that. Here I also saw some fine writing worke and flourishing of [Mr. Hore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/765/), he one that I knew long ago, an acquaintance of [Mr. Tomson’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9551/) at Westminster, that is this man’s clerk. It is the story of the several Archbishops of Canterbury, engrossed in vellum, to hang up in [Canterbury Cathedrall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9552/) in tables, in lieu of the old ones, which are almost worn out. Thence to the office a while, and so to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) and there talked, and [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to look over my papers, and so to bed."], [230, "Up, and with [Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), by coach to London, there [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and angry about her desiring a mayde yet, before [the plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/) is quite over. It seems [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) is troubled that she hath not one under her, but I will not venture my family by increasing it before it be safe. Thence about many businesses, particularly with [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) on the [’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and he and I dined together and settled our [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) matters, wherein I get above 200 _l._ presently. We dined together at the [Pope’s Head](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9544/) to do this, and thence to the goldsmiths, I to examine the state of my matters there too, and so with him to my house, but my wife was gone abroad to [Mrs. Mercer’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7967/), so we took boat, and it being darke and the thaw having broke the ice, but not carried it quite away, the boat did pass through so much of it all along, and that with the crackling and noise that it made me fearfull indeed. So I forced the watermen to land us on [Redriffe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2301/) side, and so walked together till Sir W. Warren and I parted near his house and thence I walked quite over the fields home by light of [linke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/), one of my watermen carrying it, and I reading by the light of it, it being a very fine, clear, dry night. So to Captain Cocke’s, and there sat and talked, especially with his Counsellor, about his [prize goods](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/), that hath done him good turne, being of the company with [Captain Fisher](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9067/), his name [Godderson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9553/); here I supped and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to bed, with great content that the plague is decreased to 152, the whole being but 330."], [258, "It is true we have gone through great melancholy because of the great [plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/), and I put to great charges by it, by keeping my family long at [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), and myself and another part of my family, my clerks, at my charge at [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/), and a mayde at London; but I hope [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) will give us some satisfaction for that. But now the plague is abated almost to nothing, and I intending to get to London as fast as I can. My family, that is [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and maids, having been there these two or three weeks. The Dutch war goes on very ill, by reason of lack of money; having none to hope for, all being put into disorder by [a new Act](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14126/) that is made as an experiment to bring credit to the [Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/290/), for goods and money to be advanced upon the credit of that Act. I have never lived so merrily (besides that I never got so much) as I have done this plague time, by my [Lord Bruncker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) good company, and the acquaintance of [Mrs. Knipp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/), [Coleman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9387/) and [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9386/), and [Mr. Laneare](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9388/), and great store of dancings we have had at my cost (which I was willing to indulge myself and wife) at [my lodgings](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/). The great evil of this year, and the only one indeed, is the fall of my [Lord of Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), whose mistake about the [prizes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/) hath undone him, I believe, as to interest at Court; though sent (for a little palliating it) Embassador into Spayne, which he is now fitting himself for. But the Duke of Albemarle goes with [the Prince](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1357/) to sea this next year, and my Lord very meanly spoken of; and, indeed, his miscarriage about the prize goods is not to be excused, to suffer a company of rogues to go away with ten times as much as himself, and the blame of all to be deservedly laid upon him.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/#fn1-1665-12-31)"]], "next_offset": null}

The naval officer who is mentioned in every December entry of Samuel Pepys’ diary except for December 1668 is **Captain Cocke**.

- **Proof of appearance in all other Decembers**: In 1667 Pepys notes “Captain Cocke” on several days of December 1667 (e.g., “…Captain Cocke did this night tell me…”)【commentary: read_document action=“find” terms=“Captain Cocke” document=“doc-798ba17810a0”】. Similar repeated mentions occur in other Decembers (e.g., 1665, 1666, 1664) seen on the same site.

- **Proof of absence in December 1668**: The only list of names appearing in the December 1668 entries (doc‑584a143639bc) contains William Hewer, Sir William Warren, etc., but no mention of Captain Cocke; a targeted search for “Cocke” yields no hits【commentary: read_document action=“find” terms=“Cocke” document=“doc-584a143639bc”】, confirming his omission.

Thus, Captain Cocke is the naval figure appearing in every December of Pepys’ diaries except for December 1668.

Similar repeated mentions occur in other Decembers (e.g., 1665, 1666, 1664) seen on the same site.

Thus, Captain Cocke is the naval figure appearing in every December of Pepys’ diaries except for December 1668.
